displayQuote: The Hardest Thing in the World to Understand Is Income Taxes

meta.title: Who really said “The Hardest Thing in the World to Understand Is Income Taxes”? | Quotle.info
meta.description: Probably Einstein. His own tax accountant, Leo Mattersdorf, reported the remark in a 1963 letter to Time — eight years after Einstein’s death.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said ‘The Hardest Thing in the World to Understand Is Income Taxes’?
meta.ogDescription: Reported by Einstein’s tax accountant in a 1963 letter to Time. A credible first-hand account, but recorded only after his death.

answer.label: Attributed to Albert Einstein
answer.sourceLine: The source is a letter from Leo Mattersdorf published in Time on 22 February 1963. Mattersdorf prepared Einstein’s tax returns for years, and described hearing the line over lunch at the Einsteins’ Princeton home. It is a first-hand account from someone demonstrably close to Einstein — but it was written down only after Einstein had died, so it rests on one man’s memory.
answer.confidenceText: A named first-hand witness, but recorded eight years after Einstein’s death.

source.heading: The source

docMeta.dd: Lunch at the Einstein home in Princeton

source.excerpt: One year while I was at his Princeton home preparing his return, Mrs. Einstein, who was then still living, asked me to stay for lunch. During the course of the meal, the professor turned to me and with his inimitable chuckle said: “The hardest thing in the world to understand is income taxes.” I replied: “There is one thing more difficult, and that is your theory of relativity.” “Oh, no,” he replied, “that is easy.” To which Mrs. Einstein commented, “Yes, for you.”
trail: Quote Investigator reproduces Mattersdorf’s 1963 letter to Time in full, including his statement that ‘from the time Professor Einstein came to this country until his death, I prepared his income tax returns and advised him on his tax problems’. Read the investigation ↗

Quote Investigator corroborates the relationship independently of the anecdote: Mattersdorf thanked Einstein for reading his manuscript in his 1952 book Insight into Astronomy, and Mattersdorf’s 1985 New York Times obituary records that the book was proofread by Einstein, who was his accounting client for many years. The corroborating citations ↗
Wikiquote lists the line among Einstein’s attributed material, citing the same Mattersdorf letter of 22 February 1963 — not among his sourced quotations. Wikiquote: Albert Einstein ↗

Quote Investigator’s conclusion is careful: the earliest known citation postdates Einstein’s death, and ‘the accuracy of the anecdote depends on the memory and veracity of Leo Mattersdorf’. QI’s conclusion ↗
source.excerptNote: Mattersdorf’s letter to Time, 22 February 1963. Note the wording: ‘income taxes’. The version that circulates today usually reads ‘the income tax’, a change that appears later.

author.name: Albert Einstein
author.heading: About Albert Einstein
author.bio: Albert Einstein reshaped physics with the special and general theories of relativity and won the 1921 Nobel Prize in Physics for his work on the photoelectric effect. He settled in Princeton, New Jersey in 1933 and remained there until his death in 1955. He is also the most over-attributed person in the English language — which is what makes the rare quip with a real witness behind it worth marking as such.

misattribution.heading: What to watch for
misattribution.intro: This one is probably genuine. The thing that goes wrong is the wording, and the confidence people place in it.

items.who: ‘The hardest thing in the world to understand is the income tax’
items.why: Mattersdorf’s 1963 letter says ‘income taxes’. The singular ‘the income tax’ appears from 1968 onward and is now the more common form. The 1968 variant ↗

Quote Investigator noted the quotation on the IRS newsroom’s ‘Tax Quotes’ page attributed flatly to Einstein, with no source. That page has since been removed. No official citation ever existed. Quote Investigator ↗

misattribution.truthLine: Very likely Einstein’s — but the only record is his accountant’s recollection, published eight years after he died. Quote Investigator ↗

context.heading: Why it mattered
lead: The joke works because of who is telling it. A man who reorganised our understanding of space and time, defeated by a tax form, is a comforting thought every April, which is exactly why the line travels and why it ended up on a government website without a citation.

What makes this case unusual is that the sourcing is better than most Einstein quips, not worse. There is a named witness with a documented professional relationship, a specific setting and a plausible exchange. What is missing is only the thing that would make it certain: any record of it while Einstein was alive.
context.pull: Better sourced than most Einstein quips — and still not certain.
